title: A Big Job With No Woman Ever In Charge — One Leader Just Dropped Out
summary:
Imagine a club with 193 member countries. The club has had a leader for 80 years — and that leader has always been a man. Michelle Bachelet wanted to change that. She is a former president of Chile, and she was trying to become the first woman to run the United Nations.

On Saturday, she quit the race. She shared the news in a video on Instagram. "Today I announced that I have decided not to continue with my candidacy," she said. She added that she did not regret trying, even if "the time was not right."

Why did she stop? On Friday, the UN Security Council held a secret vote called a straw poll. It is like a practice vote — nobody is forced to keep their choice. Out of 15 countries, Bachelet got only one vote saying "encourage." Eleven said "discourage." Three had no opinion. In July, she had six encouraging votes. In August, only two. Her support kept shrinking.

Now two women are ahead: Rebeca Grynspan from Costa Rica, with nine encouraging votes, and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett from Guyana, with eight. Other candidates are still in the race too.

To win, a candidate needs at least nine votes and no veto from the five permanent members: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The current leader, Antonio Guterres, finishes his job on December 31. He has warned that the UN is running out of money, with $1.57bn in unpaid dues.
why_it_matters: The UN makes choices that reach kids everywhere — like sending food, medicine and peacekeepers — so who leads it matters, and this story shows how hard it can be for women to reach the very top job.

background_read: The United Nations (a club of 193 countries that work together on peace, health and helping people) started in 1945, after World War II.
Its top job is called Secretary-General, and in 80 years no woman has ever held it.
The Security Council has 15 members, and five of them — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — are permanent members who can block a choice with a veto.

perspectives.description: They think it is unfair that no woman has led the UN in 80 years, and Bachelet said she does not regret trying even if 'the time was not right.'
They may prefer a different candidate, or they may want a leader who can fix the UN's money problems, since many countries have not paid their dues.
They point out the straw poll is only a practice vote, so the race is still open — but Rebeca Grynspan and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett now have the strongest support.
